Devastation on a low mark.
Fear of trying hard in case you are mediocre.
usual: Saying 'I worked hard, I deserve it'.
Imposter syndrome after criticism.
Half-trying to protect a self-image.
should: Confident that Allah gives khayr in any result.
Say alhamdulillah, celebrate His blessing.
Feel bad about effort, not about your worth.
At peace with being mediocre while improving.
answers: Student: confidence is knowing Allah gave the potential, vanity is the spotlight on me.
Student asked whether it is wrong to celebrate a success. He said no, celebrate Allah's blessing.

EX.title: What do I expect from Allah?
EX.instr: Think through your side of the relationship: what you expect from Him, what He expects from you, and what you give back.

uses.instr: Think through your side of the relationship: what you expect from Him, what He expects from you, and what you give back.
feel: A student felt it was wrong to expect anything.
should: Unreasonable expectations ruin any relationship, so state them honestly.
Remember that the reward of ihsan is ihsan.

EX.title: Ithar: letting others go first
EX.instr: Notice the feeling when you race for a door, parking spot or free food. Take it if you want, but recognize the leap and calm it.

uses.instr: Notice the urge to take the first or last word, interrupt, or rush ahead of people. Let them finish and let them pass.
feel: The urge to get the first word or last word.
The urge to interrupt or prepare your reply.
Rushing while walking, then realizing late that you cut someone off.
usual: Noticing it only after it has happened.
should: Notice earlier each time until it is a reflex not to do it.
Eventually the urge goes away and you become a gentleman people enjoy meeting.
answers: One person noticed the interruption urge in conversation.
One walked fast, zigzagged and realized after that he had not let someone in.

uses.instr: When your nafs fights for something in this world, let the other person have it.
feel: The nafs attacks and fights for it.
should: Become sensitive to the urges of the nafs.

uses.instr: Notice the feeling when you race for a door, parking spot or free food. Take it if you want, but recognize the leap and calm it.
feel: Anxiety and urgency before getting it.
Slight shame once you notice.
Calm and indifference as it fades.
usual: Rushing for open doors and parking spots.
Spinning a righteous-sounding story for what you want.
should: Indifference: it does not matter if I get it.
Awareness that it is the nafs leaping, not a good reason.
No joy in giving way yet, that is a later step.
answers: Class story: a brother stood at the bus door and let everyone on. The teacher said not to do that, just recognize the leap.

EX.title: An act of service you hate
EX.instr: Pick a repeated act of service for someone else that you do not want to do. Do it every day or two until it no longer bothers you. Ask yourself why you hate it.

uses.instr: Pick a repeated act of service for someone else that you do not want to do. Do it every day or two until it no longer bothers you. Ask yourself why you hate it.
feel: You hate it, or just cannot be bothered.
The nafs resists, especially the word service.
Arguing yourself into it can make it worse.
usual: Not finding anything, since the sisters already serve constantly.
Choosing something that is not service, like running, or something too random.
should: Move from hating it to being content, not to loving it.
Realize the hate was a perception from your nafs and often just selfishness.
Notice perks: a better relationship, and a nicer day.
answers: Doing the dishes in the evening for his mother.
Teaching a sibling math.
Taking out the garbage and cleaning cat litter.
Picking up a brother for the masjid. Flipping it so he leads worked better.
Calling a relative daily, which turned into love after a week.
Getting drinks for a group of friends.
The teacher walked his sister to school at 16.

uses.instr: Keep doing it until it stops bothering you. Do not expect it in a week.
feel: Tired and reluctant on the days it comes.
Still hating it after a week.
usual: Skipping or not choosing yet.
Picking something that is not service.
should: Change your expectation: decide in advance it is part of your job.
Make the task easier, such as pairing it with something relaxing.
Notice you feel good when it is done, which is free happiness.
Expect it to take years if you indulged the dislike.
answers: Deciding on Sunday to drive his sister every day that week made him stop minding.
Sleeping early until he loved sleep, which was not service but showed the feeling can change.
Cleaning the bathroom, though bad time management made him dodge it.
Picking up other people's slack, which he said got on his nerves.
One person did not end up doing it.

uses.instr: Pick a small service to others that you dislike and do it every two or three days until you stop disliking it. Find methods to make it less annoying.
feel: Annoyance and resistance.
Doubt that it will change.
A flat indifference once it works.
usual: Doing the dishes at home.
Driving kids to school with resentment.
Admitting you still hate it.
should: Indifference, not enjoyment.
Feel that you found a method yourself.
Honesty when you still dislike it.
answers: Teacher: he once hated school drop-offs and now loves picking up his daughter on Mondays.
One student said reflecting regressed him, and the teacher said that was a good realization.

uses.instr: Report whether you stopped disliking it and why you were bothered.
feel: Annoyed by the task.
Bothered when someone reminds or expects.
Pride that you serve selflessly.
usual: Looking forward to the clean result.
Mother or family thanking or reminding.
Thinking you are better than the others at home.
should: Satisfaction from accomplishment.
No bother with reminders since you obligated yourself.
Freedom from needing credit, with humility intact.
Joy of giving without strings.
answers: One student said the clean place gives satisfaction at the end.
One student said his mother's reminders bother him, the teacher said they should not as it was self-imposed.
One said he first felt better than others, then realized he is not.

EX.title: Priority list
EX.instr: Work out where the wird (and a focused sitting once or twice a week) belongs on your priority list. Optionally write an ideal list, a reality list and the list you claim. Find what has to be done first.

uses.instr: Work out where the wird (and a focused sitting once or twice a week) belongs on your priority list. Optionally write an ideal list, a reality list and the list you claim. Find what has to be done first.
feel: You do not want to open that door because it hurts: I'll deal with it later.
You say I'm too busy, which really means it did not make the cut.
Deep down you may not believe the thing matters.
usual: Lying to yourself about what your list is.
Giving an action no number at all.
Only doing the wird in dead time like the car.
should: See that your real list is what you actually do.
Be honest, since honesty gives hope of moving it up.
Put it in a reasonable spot, not number one, so after your top items you can focus.
Recognizing the gap is 80% of the work.
answers: One found it easier at Fajr before the day started.
One said the car is his only quiet time.
One lowered his priority for sports and owns the decision.
One writes down the excuses his inner self makes.

uses.instr: For three or four days observe what you actually do. Write the ideal list (public) and the real list. Find where the wird fits and see if you can raise its number a little.
feel: Discomfort seeing the real list.
Realizing you only do the wird in dead time.
usual: Lying to yourself about it.
Giving it no number at all.
should: Honesty and acknowledgement of the gap.
Willingness to shift priorities, not guilt.

uses.instr: Observe what you do for two to three days and write the real list, then the ideal list, and ask what is missing.
feel: Discomfort and self-defense when you see the real list.
The urge to change your behavior while being observed.
Surprise that dopamine things dominate.
usual: Saying obligations are priorities but the time counts disagree.
Priorities that are seasonal or cyclical.
Noticing the gap very late in life when consequences arrive.
should: Honest observation without judgment.
Curiosity about what you truly believe versus what you prefer to spend time on.
Questioning your understanding of the missing item.
answers: One said his real priorities are anything that releases dopamine like YouTube and food.
One said he tells himself obligations are priorities but the time spent differs.
One noticed his priorities change by season.
One admitted he stopped himself from doing things so he would not have to log them.

uses.instr: Compare the ideal and real lists and ask why there is a gap. Do not only manage time, figure out what you actually believe.
feel: Eye-opening at first.
Tender and sore, like ripping off a long-worn bandage.
The pull to blame the world instead.
usual: Turning the list into a checklist and time management.
Blaming friends, parents, society or the economy.
Saying you do not agree you are wrong.
should: Hit the brakes and own it: there is no one to blame but me.
Be curious about why, not guilty.
Move beliefs from the mind to the heart.
answers: One made a checklist and found checking items off became a habit.
One asked why free time has so much value.
One said finding the answer to why I feel something is not coming.

EX.title: Dua for someone you envy or dislike
EX.instr: Pick a person who mistreated, shrugged you off or you simply envy or dislike (not a tyrant). Make dua for them. Do not be told what to ask for, work it out.

uses.instr: Pick a person who mistreated, shrugged you off or you simply envy or dislike (not a tyrant). Make dua for them. Do not be told what to ask for, work it out.
feel: Resistance and discomfort, it is hard to admit you envy someone.
Reluctance or 'not that guy'.
A bit of honest embarrassment when you notice it.
usual: Most people avoid doing it. Last time hardly anyone did.
Students pick someone extreme like an oppressor to avoid the real one.
Saying you cannot think of anyone.
should: Admit the envy or dislike to yourself first.
Choose a mild person from your real life.
Struggle with it and bring what you noticed next week.
answers: A student asked what if no one comes to mind. He replied there is always someone who misjudged or misspoke to you.

uses.instr: Pick a mild person you dislike or envy and make dua for them in detail, wishing them good with no limit. Humanize them and see where it gets stuck.
feel: Fine with a general dua, then hard when extending it.
A feeling of not wanting them to get more than you.
Saying the words without meaning them.
Painful, like climbing your own hill.
Possible relief and mercy when you imagine their hard day.
usual: Piling on benefits to push through without addressing the cause.
Finding excuses and minor details to keep disliking them.
Assuming the envied person has a perfect life.
should: Feel openness that you want good for them and are not limiting Allah's giving.
Feel rahma once you see them as human.
Recognize it is about you, not them, and they probably do not remember.
Let go of the grudge since it burns only you.
answers: One found it easier to let go.
One felt tempted to limit the dua so they do not get more than him.
One said he made detailed dua but did not mean a word.
One said it works when you think of the benefit to you.
One said envy comes from thinking they do not deserve it or they hurt you.
Teacher's story: he made dua for the teammate who ended his football career.

uses.instr: For two weeks make du'a for a regular person who does not treat you well, and really mean it.
feel: Struggle to mean it.
Heart opener when you succeed.
usual: Choosing someone mildly annoying.
should: Eye-opening and heart-softening.
answers: The teacher promised to share his own story next time.

uses.instr: Make du'a that is genuine for a regular person who mistreated you, and report what stopped you.
feel: Anger that melts when you list what they did.
Fear that it will work and they will rise.
Pity once you see their life.
Relief like a popped balloon.
usual: 'I do not care if they are guided.'
Saying you cannot do it.
Predestination used to soften the hurt.
should: Humanize: they are as weak and lost as you.
See that the struggle is within you.
Do not carry their harm as extra weight.
Wish them good without needing to forgive.
answers: One student found his reason for anger was weak after listing it.
Another said he was concerned that the person would rise if the du'a worked.
One argued it was illogical and against his interests, so the teacher pressed him to push back on himself.
Teacher's story: his tackle injury, humanizing the player, and later friendship.

EX.title: Deep reflection on hub
EX.instr: Take the concept of love and think what it means to you. Run scenarios, ask real questions, 10 to 15 minutes a day.

uses.instr: Take the concept of love and think what it means to you. Run scenarios, ask real questions, 10 to 15 minutes a day.
feel: Sitting there with no idea what to do, mind drifting.
Plateau, feeling you can go no further.
should: Ask questions you can pursue, then seek ilm when you plateau.
Check the conclusion has gone down to the heart.

EX.title: Spot your assumptions
EX.instr: Notice when you assume the worst of someone, ask what you are taking value from, and replace it with a good assumption or none.

uses.instr: Notice what you assume about a person who harmed or outdid you. Imagine the opposite and recognize neither is likely true.
feel: Certainty that the person is evil.
Defensiveness because your nafs thinks it is protecting you.
usual: Judging the whole person by one act.
Painting envied people as having no problems.
should: Soften into sympathy or empathy.
See that the truth is in the middle.
answers: Students named judgment and assumptions when asked what they had just done.

uses.instr: Pick bad assumptions, showing off or arrogance as the heart-based habit and define when and why it appears.
feel: Defensiveness and surprise at how often it happens.
Embarrassment about wanting recognition.
usual: Assuming every driver is out to get you.
Looking for recognition in recitation or leading prayer.
should: Feel watchful and calm when it arises.
Feel that Allah's approval is enough.
answers: One student chose arrogance.

uses.instr: Notice when you assume the worst of someone, ask what you are taking value from, and replace it with a good assumption or none.
feel: A small lift in self-esteem when you assume bad.
Irritation at drivers or strangers.
Guilt once you notice.
usual: Filling gaps about a stranger from their looks or job.
Assuming a cutter-off driver is evil.
Curiosity about others' private lives.
should: Calm, with no need to judge.
Good assumption: maybe a bad day.
Responsible suspicion only when you protect or teach someone (parent, teacher, business, advice).
answers: Class named when bad assumptions are needed: marriage, leadership, business and money, giving advice.
Teacher: a father must assume the worst to protect his child.

EX.title: What is joyful and what is useful
EX.instr: Separate happiness that swings your self-value from real happiness, and anger that is right from anger that is ego.

uses.instr: Identify what brings you joy and what is useful, and ask whether you can find joy in useful things.
feel: Tedium in useful tasks, joy in useless ones.
Possible quiet joy in learning or service.
should: Widen the bandwidth of your joy toward the useful.
Keep leisure but not as the only source of joy.

uses.instr: Separate happiness that swings your self-value from real happiness, and anger that is right from anger that is ego.
feel: Pride and excitement when you win or are praised.
Sadness at loss that should stay sadness.
usual: Happiness depends on something happening.
Hiding sadness or avoiding it.
should: Happiness as a state of mind.
Genuine emotion not attached to self-value.
Joy in family moments.
answers: Student asked how to differentiate. Teacher: sit and differentiate, that is the work.
Student: can you be happy that you lost? Teacher: no, be sad, just do not let it swing.

EX.title: Make a task you dislike joyful
EX.instr: Pick a purposeful task you dislike and do more than once a week: wake for Fajr and stay awake, fast, daily learning, daily exercise, or time with relatives. Make adjustments until you enjoy it.

uses.instr: Choose something meaningful and useful that you avoid, like waking early. Redesign it with several tweaks so you look forward to it. Run the idea past the teacher.
feel: Dread and avoidance at first.
Mild excitement once the attached reward exists.
Joy emerges later from the meaning itself.
usual: Picking something trivial like flash cards.
Looking for one switch instead of many tweaks.
Using only rewards, which fade.
should: Feel purposeful and look forward to the task.
See yourself as getting a privilege, not carrying a chore.
Notice that meaning itself becomes the joy over time.
answers: One student suggested flash cards and was told it is not clearly purposeful.
One student's idea: waking early plus a pleasant breakfast or seeing someone.
One student said things he hated became fun once he saw them as time with his dad.
Students linked fun to ease, accomplishment, pleasure, stimulation, competition and feedback.

uses.instr: Pick a purposeful task you dislike and do more than once a week: wake for Fajr and stay awake, fast, daily learning, daily exercise, or time with relatives. Make adjustments until you enjoy it.
feel: The first days hurt, like missing the lunchtime tea.
Resistance and the nafs saying later.
Relief after two or three days.
usual: Choosing the easy one or ranking the one you dread last.
Thinking it will just work by commitment.
Rushing into it without adjustments, like migraines from fasting.
should: Feel honest about 'I just do not want to'.
Feel the task becoming enjoyable with tweaks, then independent of them.
Feel an investment paying off, not a punishment.
answers: One student picked fasting twice a week.

One said fasting gave him migraines and he realized he needed better planning.
One said he does it for the teacher as motivation.
One suggested a group camp.

uses.instr: Report on the exercise: what adjustments you made, what changed.
feel: Surprise at forgetting why you hated it after the first two days.
Blind effort without a plan feels hard.
Better days and more done once earlier.
usual: Setting an alarm and trying to wake only, with no other change.
Not thinking about why before starting.
should: Feel the day improve and joy forming with small adjustments.
Feel convinced by the evidence you gathered.
answers: One student's alarm approach worked once he also slept earlier and prayed Fajr early.
One fasted two days and forgot why he hated it.
One said the weekday is harder because he dislikes school.
One slept through the alarm after the first day then adjusted.

uses.instr: Make small chained adjustments, write them down, attach something halal you enjoy, then invest in the task itself.
feel: Mixed: dread, then lightness once chained adjustments work.
Failure feeling when you slip, tempting you to blame 'some reason'.
Some mild guilt about attaching a reward, which he says is unnecessary.
usual: Waking early without sleeping early.
Fasting from Fajr while keeping the day packed.
Dropping the habit when the reward is removed.
should: Feel that the action itself is not the problem, your context is.
Feel at ease attaching enjoyment, with Allah knowing you are weak.
Feel growing joy from investing in the task.
answers: One put the alarm far away.

One started sleeping hungry to make suhoor easy.
One planned soccer after Fajr.
One said reading a section on prayer improved focus but it faded in days.

uses.instr: Make small adjustments (ripple effect) and add an association (a carrot behind the deed). Use the grace period to invest in the deed itself.
feel: Truce with the nafs once something it likes is attached.
Feeling that scheduling is a puzzle you solve.
A sense of being bored of the carrot after a while.
usual: Setting an earlier wake time without moving sleep or evening activities.
Swapping rewards again and again.
Calling cutting scrolling a large adjustment.
should: Feel fighting less and enjoying more.
Feel the deed cemented in your schedule.
Feel prepared for Ramadan.
answers: One student needs a great day to end on a high, then stays up late.
One student attached soccer to Fajr.
One said his brother in the military must go to the gym daily so he can put it after Fajr.

EX.title: Write your Ramadan plan and bad habit list

feel: Overwhelm when too ambitious.
Embarrassment seeing screen time numbers.
usual: Writing a vague goal like be closer to Allah.
Writing a one-word bad habit like scrolling.

Feel that ambition is better than idle time.
answers: One student checked his iPhone screen time and found it unreasonable.
One shared an app that forces you to write an intention before opening social media.

feel: Resistance to naming things precisely.
Embarrassment about sharing.
Anxiety about too much to fit.
usual: Vague habits such as scrolling or swearing.

Copying someone else's list.

Feel pulled out from time wasters without burning bridges.
Feel prepared rather than overwhelmed.
answers: One said he scrolls before sleep on Instagram 30 to 45 minutes.

One said he must watch a YouTube video for 10 minutes before studying.
One said not building his day around salah is his bad habit while another disagreed.

EX.title: Should you hope others do better than you?
EX.instr: Answer why the nafs compares and whether you should wish others to do better, then try wishing it.

uses.instr: If you feel equal, ask whether you should hope others do better. Test it by trying the opposite.
feel: Awkward at hoping someone else does better.
Competitive pull.

Quiet envy.
should: Hope for their good, or do not concern yourself with their path.

uses.instr: Answer why the nafs compares and whether you should wish others to do better, then try wishing it.

Quiet burning while smiling at someone's success.
Lightness once comparison stops.
usual: Wanting to be the best and others behind.
Excuses about others' background and genetics.

EX.title: 'I would never do that' versus 'I pray I never do that'

Mercy for the person while still opposing harm.

Another asked if arrogance gets harder with age or status.

EX.title: Serve everyone and test your nafs

Awareness that you may have been comparing.
usual: Looking down on people with less guidance or knowledge.
Envy of people more guided.

EX.title: Think of a blessing at sami'a Allahu liman hamidah

PH.title: Foundations
PH.blurb: How the halaqa runs, why a deed can be done well and still not be accepted, and fixing the intention.
body: The first three lessons set the frame. The group is small, closed to drop-ins, and each week runs through four fixed segments: comprehension, connection, ritual and exercises.
The core idea is servanthood (abd): you are a servant whether you like it or not, and the work is to choose it. Asking 'am I serving Allah or serving myself?' is the question to return to for life.
Lesson 2 explains qabool al-amal, that acceptance is a separate matter from doing a deed perfectly. Lesson 3 turns to tashih al-niyyah, improving the quality of the intention before acting.
Practice starts light: a small daily wird attached to a prayer, kept for 15 days, plus a pause before salah.
PH.next: These ideas are the ground for ihsan and the exercises in the next stretch.

PH.title: Excellence and service
PH.blurb: Ihsan, preferring others (ithar), doing what you dislike, and staying consistent under stress.
body: Lesson 4 completes the four comprehension ideas with ihsan, excellence in the relationship with Allah and with people, and what expectations come with each.
Lessons 5 and 6 turn to practice. Ithar means letting others go first and finish speaking. The 'do what you dislike' exercise is used to watch a feeling move from hating something to not hating it.
The wird is explained as training to commit to something optional and be consistent, before focus or meaning are added.
PH.next: With consistency in place, the course moves to what you value and how you spend time.

PH.title: Time, value and love
PH.blurb: Why valued actions get time, what you really love, the hadith of the sweetness of iman, and the gap between knowing and doing.
body: Lesson 7 asks why the wird is easier on the run and harder when you sit down: the action is not valued enough. The priority list is introduced to compare what you claim matters with where your time goes.
Lessons 8 and 9 recap the four basics and debrief the du'a for someone you dislike, looking at what people felt and why it got hard. Lesson 10 says tazkiyah has no stages or levels.

Lessons 11 and 12 finish the hadith of the sweetness of iman (loving Allah and His Messenger most, loving people for Allah, hating to return to disbelief) and debrief the priority list around the real question: why is there a gap between what I know is right and what I do?
PH.next: Understanding the gap leads to joy, purpose and small adjustments.

PH.title: Purpose and small adjustments
PH.blurb: Joy and focus, choosing a purposeful task you dislike, making it doable, and defining bad habits.
body: Lesson 13 debriefs the joy and fun reflection: what makes something fun and what it means to focus through joy. Lesson 14 explains that exercises exist to teach you something about yourself, not to tick a box.

Lessons 15, 17 and 18 run the 'make a disliked task joyful' exercise through small adjustments (timing, what it attaches to), including preparing for Ramadan. Lesson 16 introduces the low end of the pendulum, low self-esteem.
Lesson 19 teaches defining a bad habit precisely: what, when, where, how long, why.
PH.next: Knowing the pendulum and your habits sets up the revision cycle and the work on self-value.

PH.title: Self-value, humbleness and the ego
PH.blurb: The revision cycle, the pendulum, vanity and arrogance, Iblis, tasbih, and gratitude.
body: Lesson 20 starts a revision cycle: two of the four categories per sitting, completing in roughly ten weeks. Each topic returns every two weeks.
Lessons 21 and 22 develop self-value: vanity and arrogance sit on the same swing as low self-esteem, and a good assumption about people helps keep the pendulum steady.

Lesson 23 explains why the halaqa exists, with a method of creed, fiqh and suluk. Lesson 24 finishes the Iblis case study, which shows how arrogance grows into something large. Lesson 25 teaches tasbih as the core of aqidah, gratitude (hamd), and the du'a debrief.
PH.next: With arrogance understood, the course asks where humbleness is needed in your own life.

PH.title: Boundaries, sins and emotions
PH.blurb: Humbleness examples, triggers, tawbah with a plan, the black box of belief, and healthy versus toxic emotions.
body: Lessons 26 and 28 gather real examples of where humbleness matters (compliments, criticism, creative work, religiosity) and define boundaries as triggers, what makes you swing.
Lesson 27 teaches self-solving and works on sujud du'a, recording sins and the first steps of tawbah.

Lessons 29 and 31 teach tawbah as regret, stopping, and a plan, and introduce the black box: what you tell people, what you tell yourself, and what you really believe. Lesson 30 sets the group rules and takes the pendulum in both directions.
Lesson 32 treats emotions: swing-generated emotion is unhealthy by default, genuine emotion is not tied to self-value, and khushu' depends on that.

PH.title: Honesty, emotion and death
PH.blurb: A tawbah plan and the sunnah of Fajr, genuine emotion, then imagining your own death and what fulfilment means.

PH.title: Mortality
PH.blurb: Accepting mortality, the ruh and the nafs, walking the path without owning the outcome, and death as a transition.

PH.title: Contemplation and salah
PH.blurb: Learning tafakkur, catching ideas, the three goals of tazkiyah, and contemplating the concepts of salah.

PH.blurb: Hasad through Qabil and Habil and Yusuf's brothers, the cure of jama'a, and ghibta versus hasad.
